claims.text: The coating consists of alternating near-equiatomic high-entropy-alloy layers deposited by physical vapor deposition.
Varying individual layer thickness while holding total coating thickness constant changes the density of multilayer interfaces.
High-density, chemically heterogeneous interfaces govern the coating's resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Multilayer interfaces introduce chemical and structural heterogeneity.
Multilayer interfaces modify local strain fields and generate local stress gradients.
The interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The interfaces impede dislocation propagation by forcing dislocations to change paths or become absorbed.
Restricted dislocation nucleation and propagation reduce the rate of plastic deformation.
Interface-associated stress gradients may promote limited recovery or self-healing through enhanced diffusion.
Interface-promoted recovery or self-healing contributes to improved creep resistance.
Thinner individual layers, and therefore higher interface density, will produce lower creep strain rates than thicker-layer coatings.
Higher-interface-density multilayers will have lower creep strain rates than a homogeneous HEA coating of comparable composition and thickness.
The proposed behavior applies when dislocation-mediated plasticity is the dominant high-temperature creep mechanism.
The proposed behavior applies only before interface instability or phase segregation occurs.
Interface degradation or diffusion-induced coarsening at sufficiently high temperature may eliminate the proposed benefit.
The relative contributions of interface density and interface-enhanced diffusion are quantitatively uncertain.
